events.determination_commission_division: Determination made by Commissioner Williams pursuant to a delegation under section 25(1) of the Act

determination_table_content.details:
SMG-Three LLC (SMG-Three) and Sony Music Publishing (SMP)
(together Sony Music) propose to acquire 100% of the shares of
Recognition Music Group (Delaware) L.P. (Recognition Music)
(together, the Parties) from funds advised and/or managed by
Blackstone, Inc. (the Acquisition).

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission has
determined under section 51ABZE(1) of the Competition and
Consumer Act 2010 (Cth) that the Acquisition may be put into effect.

The acquirer, Sony Music, acquires and commercialises music
publishing rights, including performing and mechanical rights, online
rights, synchronisation rights and print rights.
The target, Recognition Music, holds music publishing rights.
The Parties overlap in the supply of music publishing services.

When making a determination in Phase 1, the Australian Competition
and Consumer Commission (ACCC) undertakes a competition
assessment and considers whether it is appropriate for an
acquisition to be approved or subject to further assessment in
Phase 2 in accordance with section 51ABZJ of the Competition and
Consumer Act 2010 (Cth) (the Act). In doing so, the ACCC must have
regard to the object of the Act and all relevant matters, including the
interests of consumers.
For more information about the ACCC’s approach to considering
notified acquisitions, see the ACCC’s merger assessment guidelines
and interim merger process guidelines.
In conducting its competition assessment, the ACCC has considered
the information and documents that were submitted with the
notification form and by third parties, information from prior and
current other matters and publicly available information.
The ACCC has determined that the Acquisition may be put into
effect as it considers that the Acquisition is unlikely to have the
effect of substantially lessening competition in any market. In
reaching its decision, and based on the material before it, the ACCC
makes the following findings.
• The merged firm would continue to face competition from
alternative suppliers of music publishing services in Australia
and globally including Universal Music, Warner Music and BMG,
amongst others.
• Post-acquisition, Sony is unlikely to have the ability and incentive
to bundle or tie its supply of artist and repertoire services to its
supply of music publishing services with the effect of
substantially lessening competition or foreclose rivals’ access to
music in the movie and gaming industries as it will continue to
face competition from the other suppliers, as mentioned above.

A notifying party, or other person who has been allowed to do so by
the Australian Competition Tribunal, may apply for review if they are
dissatisfied with the determination. Pursuant to section 100C of the
Act, applications for review of the determination are to be made to
the Australian Competition Tribunal before the end of 14 calendar
days after this statement of reasons was included on the ACCC’s
Acquisitions Register. To confirm whether there has been any
application for review, please contact the Australian Competition
Tribunal.

shares in Ace Communication Distributors Pty Ltd (Ace) (the
Acquisition).

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission has
determined under section 51ABZE(1) of the Competition and
Consumer Act 2010 (Cth) that the Acquisition may be put into effect.

The acquirer, Logic, is a wholesale distributor of certain
communication equipment, operating across Australia and New
Zealand. Logic supplies two-way radio infrastructure and terminals,
push-to-talk over cellular devices, dispatch software, video security
systems and audio accessories.
The target, Ace, is an Australian wholesale distributor of wireless
communication technologies, including two-way radio products,
push-to-talk over cellular devices and body worn cameras. Ace also
provides services in design, consulting, radio licensing, software
support and product training.
The reasons for the ACCC’s determination are set out in section 2.

determination_statement_of_reasons.text: When making a determination in Phase 1, the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) undertakes a competition assessment and considers whether it is appropriate for an acquisition to be approved or subject to further assessment in Phase 2 in accordance with section 51ABZJ of the Competition and Consumer Act 2010 (Cth) (the Act). In doing so, the ACCC must have regard to the object of the Act and all relevant matters, including the interests of consumers.
For more information about the ACCC’s approach to considering notified acquisitions, see the ACCC’s merger assessment guidelines and interim merger process guidelines.
Overlap and relationship between the parties

Logic and Ace (the Parties) overlap in the wholesale distribution of certain communications equipment in Australia, including two-way radio and push-to-talk over cellular products (together, Critical Communication Products). This includes handsets, accessories (headphones, microphones, chargers and batteries) as well as infrastructure equipment (antennae, switches, repeaters, servers and related software). Logic and Ace are the only two distributors of Motorola Critical Communication Products in Australia but Ace also distributes other brands of Critical Communication Products.

Logic is vertically integrated in that its parent company, CSE Group Limited (CSE Group), operates reseller businesses1 that acquire Critical Communication Products from Logic (and other distributors such as Ace) for re-supply to end users. CSE Group’s related reseller businesses sell Critical Communication Products manufactured by various brands, including Motorola, Tait, Kenwood and Hytera.
Industry background

Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs) such as Motorola Solutions Inc (Motorola) design and manufacture critical communication products, such as two- way radios, and push-to-talk over cellular products.

items: Two-way radios are communication devices that can both transmit and receive radio waves, allowing individuals to talk bidirectionally. Two-way radios may be handheld or installed in vehicles. For radios to operate, they must be supported by a radio network or infrastructure hosted on towers or buildings to project the frequency across a wide area that the radios can connect to.

Push-to-talk over cellular products are communication devices that leverage cellular networks and Wi-Fi for wide area radio communication. They do not require a radio network or infrastructure as they operate via the existing cellular 4G/5G/Long-Term Evolution (LTE) technology and Wi-Fi networks.

determination_statement_of_reasons.text: Distributors, such as Logic and Ace, purchase bulk Critical Communication Products from the OEMs and hold stock to provide timely delivery to authorised resellers. Resellers either purchase products directly from the OEMs or through distributors and then sell to end users.
Competition assessment

The ACCC has considered the effects of the Acquisition by comparing the likely future state of competition if the Acquisition proceeds against the continuation of the current state of competition (being the likely future state of competition if the Acquisition does not proceed).
The ACCC has considered whether the Acquisition is likely to substantially lessen competition by:

items: substantially reducing competitive constraint which would enable the merged entity to increase prices of Motorola Critical Communication Products, by reducing the discount premiums that would otherwise be provided to resellers of these products,

providing the merged entity with the ability and incentive to foreclose rival Critical Communication Product resellers’ access to Motorola Critical Communication Products by delaying supply and limiting price discounts to rival resellers, and/or
providing the merged entity with access to competitively significant information about rival resellers, that it would not have, absent the Acquisition.

determination_statement_of_reasons.text: The ACCC’s assessment regarding each of these points is discussed further below. 1 CSE Crosscom, Gencom, Marcom Watson and Gambier Electronics
Relevant areas of competition

The ACCC has considered the effect of the Acquisition on competition in the supply of Critical Communication Products, being two-way radio and push-to-talk over cellular products in Australia, to resellers as well as to end customers. For the purposes of this assessment, it was not necessary to reach a definitive view on the precise product market, as it does not materially alter the ACCC’s competition assessment.
Horizontal unilateral effects in the wholesale supply of Critical Communication Products in Australia

The ACCC considers that the Acquisition is unlikely to have the effect of substantially lessening competition in relation to the wholesale supply of Critical Communication Products to resellers in Australia by combining the only two wholesale suppliers of Motorola Critical Communication Products.
In reaching its decision, and based on the materials before it, the ACCC makes the following findings:

items.text: There are multiple suppliers of Critical Communication Products in Australia, with the products being differentiated, for example in functionality, support and service.

The Parties are close competitors in the supply of Critical Communication Products, as they are the only two wholesale suppliers of Motorola Communications Products in Australia and the Acquisition would remove competition between them.
There is some competition from distributors of other brands of Critical Communication Products.

The merged entity would likely be constrained by timely and sufficient entry into the wholesale or retail supply of Motorola Critical Communication Products as Motorola would be able to sponsor new entry or enter itself. The ACCC considers that Motorola would have the ability and incentive to appoint additional distributors and/or, supply products directly in Australia itself if Logic were to substantially increase prices to resellers post- Acquisition.

determination_statement_of_reasons.text: The ACCC has had regard to feedback received from third parties regarding the impact of the Acquisition. Some submitted that the Acquisition would not impact competition as Motorola exercises a significant degree of control over the distribution of its Critical Communication Products in Australia and there is no commercial benefit from acquiring products from one distributor over the other.

However, other third parties emphasised the strong position of Motorola Critical Communication Products, the importance to resellers of access to those products on commercially acceptable terms for re-supply and concerns that independent resellers could be foreclosed as a result of Logic’s increased vertical integration through its related reseller businesses.

Ultimately, having regard to the material before the ACCC as a whole, there was insufficient evidence to indicate that these factors are likely to have the effect of substantially lessening competition.
Non-horizontal effects – foreclosure of rival resellers in the supply of Critical Communications Products in Australia

The ACCC considers that the Acquisition is unlikely to result in the merged entity having the ability and incentive to foreclose rivals to CSE Group that resell Critical Communication Products by delaying, limiting or withholding supply or by raising prices of Motorola products to rival resellers, for example by limiting discounts. The ACCC considered this potential effect of the Acquisition in the downstream resale of Motorola Critical Communication Products based on feedback they are an essential product for downstream resellers.

Based on third party feedback and information provided by the Parties, the ACCC finds that the merged entity is unlikely to have the ability to fully or partly foreclose rivals to CSE Group. If Logic were to engage in input or customer foreclosure in a way that reduced sales of Motorola Critical Communication Products in Australia, the ACCC considers that Motorola would have the ability and incentive to pursue alternative means of distribution, including by appointing additional distributors and supplying products directly in Australia.

As the ACCC considers that the merged entity is unlikely to have the ability to foreclose rival Critical Communication Product resellers, it was not necessary to consider whether it would have the incentive to engage in such a strategy or whether it could have the effect of substantially lessening competition.
Non-horizontal effects – reduced competition arising from CSE Group accessing and using competitively significant information about rival resellers

The ACCC considers that the Acquisition is unlikely to have the effect of substantially lessening competition in the wholesale supply of Critical Communication Products in Australia as a result of CSE Group’s access to and use of competitively significant information about rival resellers post-Acquisition through Ace’s distribution arrangements with those resellers.

Based on information provided by the Parties and third parties, the ACCC understands that post-Acquisition, CSE Group via Logic could have access to additional information regarding resellers’ Critical Communication Products sales, that it does not currently have access to.

The ACCC’s view, based on the information received by the Parties and third parties, is that while some data that Logic (and therefore CSE Group), would receive post- Acquisition may provide insights relating to resellers’ orders and sales volumes, subject to limited exceptions, the type of data that it may receive does not appear to be competitively significant such that it would undermine CSE Group’s rivals’ ability or incentives to compete effectively. This is because, based on the materials before it, the ACCC understands that this information is relatively general in nature, and does not generally include information such as reseller pricing, customers, bids or opportunities.

The ACCC is also aware that in limited circumstances, Logic could receive access to end user and opportunity information, that is likely to be competitively significant. However, the ACCC finds that if the merged entity were to use competitively significant information about rival resellers to undermine rivals’ ability or incentive to compete effectively, for the reasons set out at paragraph 2.17 above, Motorola has the ability and incentive to prevent this by pursuing alternative means of distribution, including appointing additional distributors and supplying products in Australia itself.

determination_table_content.details:
Groupe Bruxelles Lambert SA (together with its subsidiaries, GBL),
alongside certain funds managed and/or advised by CVC Capital
Partners plc (the CVC Funds) indirectly, applied, through Respighi
Bidco S.p.A (Bidco), for a notification waiver in respect of their
proposed acquisition of all outstanding shares of Recordati S.p.A.
(Recordati), as described in the transaction documents provided as
part of the application (the Acquisition).
Following completion of the Acquisition, GBL will have a
shareholding of approximately 30% in TopCo with the acquiring CVC
Funds holding the remainder, subject to a small amount of shares
held by Mr Andrea Recordati.

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission has
determined under section 51ABV(1)(a) of the Competition and
Consumer Act 2010 (Cth) that the Acquisition is not required to be
notified.
30 June 2026

The acquirer, Bidco, is indirectly but wholly owned by Respighi Topco
Sarl (TopCo). TopCo is in turn held by the CVC Funds. The CVC
Network is a global alternative investment manager focused on
private equity, credit, infrastructure and secondaries, and includes
CVC Capital Partners plc, each of its subsidiaries from time to time
and the CVC Funds. Relevantly, the CVC network’s portfolio includes
interests in companies active within the pharmaceutical industry.
GBL is a publicly listed investment holding company headquartered
in Brussels. GBL invests in global companies operating in various
sectors, mainly headquartered in Europe, and relies on a stable and
supportive family shareholder base.
The target, Recordati, is headquartered in Milan and is an
international pharmaceutical group dedicated to the research,
development, manufacturing and marketing of pharmaceuticals.
Recordati has operations throughout the whole of Europe, Turkey,
North Africa, the US, Canada, Mexico, South America, Japan,
Australia, New Zealand, China and South Korea.
Recordati offers a range of pharmaceuticals across two segments:
(i) Specialty & Primary Care and (ii) Rare Diseases. Recordati also
produces several active ingredients and intermediates in its two
pharmaceutical chemical production plants. These are mainly used
in the production of some of the key products in the portfolio, but in
part are also sold externally to other pharmaceutical companies.

In making this notification waiver determination, the Australian
Competition and Consumer Commission (the ACCC) has considered
the information provided with the notification waiver application, and
had regard to the factors in section 51ABV(2)(b) of the Competition
and Consumer Act 2010 (Cth) (the Act).
Based on the information currently before it, the ACCC considers
that the Acquisition is unlikely to give rise to any material lessening
of competition. In particular,
a. the CVC Funds already control Recordati, and the Acquisition
does not create any new horizontal overlap between CVC
Capital Partners and Recordati in the supply of
pharmaceuticals in Australia
b. there is no horizontal overlap between GBL’s portfolio
companies and Recordati in the supply of pharmaceuticals
in Australia.
The ACCC has also had regard to the likelihood that, if the
Acquisition were put into effect, the notification thresholds
determined under section 51ABP(1) of the Act would apply.
While the ACCC considers that the notification thresholds are likely
to be met, given that material competition concerns are unlikely to
arise, the ACCC has determined that the Acquisition is not required
to be notified.
The ACCC considers that the determination is consistent with the
object of the Act and the interests of consumers in promoting
competition.
For more information about the ACCC’s approach to considering
notification waiver applications and to assessing competition
effects more generally, see the ACCC’s interim guidance on
notification waivers and merger assessment guidelines.

determination_table_content.details:
Service Stream Limited (Service Stream), via a wholly owned
subsidiary, proposes to acquire all of the issued share capital in RiE
Group Pty Ltd (RiE).

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission has
determined under section 51ABZE(1) of the Competition and
Consumer Act 2010 (Cth) that the Acquisition may be put into effect.

The acquirer, Service Stream, provides asset lifecycle services
through various subsidiaries, specialising in the design, construction,
operation, and maintenance of essential infrastructure networks
across all States and Territories in Australia. Service Stream’s
business is divided into three operating divisions, which are
Telecommunications, Transport and Utilities.
Service Stream’s Utilities division, which is relevant to the proposed
acquisition, provides services to the water, power and industrial
sectors, including:
• design, civil, structural, electrical, mechanical, control
engineering and metering services to the water industry
• operations, maintenance, design and installation services in
relation to gas assets
• distribution and metering services for electricity networks
including network maintenance, asset inspection and
installation services.
The target, RiE, is a privately-owned industrial electrical and
instrumentation provider based in Queensland’s Western Downs
region. RiE offers specialised electrical and instrumentation
infrastructure services, equipment rental and labour hire solutions
targeted to industrial clients who rely on electrical infrastructure to
operate their plant or facilities. RiE’s clients operate in fields such as
power generation, renewable energy, oil and gas, and utilities.

determination_table_content.item:
Overlap and relationship
between the parties
determination_table_content.details:
The parties overlap in the supply of electrical and instrumentation
(E&I) services. However, Service Stream and RiE’s operations have
minimal overlap as Service Stream provides limited E&I services to
only one customer in Queensland. RiE provides E&I services to
multiple customers in the industrial sector in Queensland and New
South Wales.

When making a determination in Phase 1, the Australian Competition
and Consumer Commission (ACCC) undertakes a competition
assessment and considers whether it is appropriate for an
acquisition to be approved or subject to further assessment in
Phase 2 in accordance with section 51ABZJ of the Competition and
Consumer Act 2010 (Cth) (the Act). In doing so, the ACCC must have
regard to the object of the Act and all relevant matters, including the
interests of consumers.
For more information about the ACCC’s approach to considering
notified acquisitions, see the ACCC’s merger assessment guidelines
and interim merger process guidelines.
In conducting its competition assessment, the ACCC has considered
the information and documents that were submitted with the
notification form and information from third parties.
The ACCC has determined that the Acquisition may be put into
effect as it considers that the Acquisition is unlikely to have the
effect of substantially lessening competition in any market. In
reaching its decision, and based on the material before it, the ACCC
makes the following findings.
• Service Stream and RiE do not compete closely in the supply of
E&I services.
• the market share aggregation resulting from the Acquisition in
the supply of E&I services is estimated to be minimal.
• Service Stream would likely continue to be constrained by
multiple alternative suppliers of E&I services.

A notifying party, or other person who has been allowed to do so by
the Australian Competition Tribunal, may apply for review if they are
dissatisfied with the determination. Pursuant to section 100C of the
Act, applications for review of the determination are to be made to
the Australian Competition Tribunal before the end of 14 calendar
days after this statement of reasons was included on the ACCC’s
Acquisitions Register. To confirm whether there has been any
application for review, please contact the Australian Competition
Tribunal.

determination_table_content.details:
Freedom Fuels Australia Pty Ltd (Freedom Fuels) applied for a
notification waiver in respect of its proposed acquisition of the
operating rights and equipment for the 'Connetic' fuel retail site
operated by Rennic Pty Ltd (Rennic) in Armidale, NSW, as described
in the transaction documents provided as part of the application (the
Acquisition).

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission has
determined under section 51ABV(1)(a) of the Competition and
Consumer Act 2010 (Cth) that the Acquisition is not required to be
notified.
3 July 2026

The acquirer, Freedom Fuels, is a small to medium sized,
independent fuel business that operates across the fuel wholesale,
fuel distribution and fuel retail markets in Eastern Australia. Freedom
Fuels is wholly owned by Idemitsu Kosan Co. Ltd – a Japanese
energy company.
Together with its sister company Trinity Petroleum Services Pty Ltd,
Freedom Fuels operates 54 fuel retail sites in total – 52 in
Queensland and two in the Northern Rivers Region of NSW (located
in Kingscliff and Terranora). Freedom Fuels also operates a fuel
wholesale business in Queensland, NSW and Victoria.
The vendor, Rennic, is a small, independent fuel business that has
been divesting its fuel retail sites in recent years. Rennic's sole
remaining fuel retail site is located in Armidale NSW, which operates
under a trademark registered to Rennic ('Connetic').
Freedom Fuels has previously been a wholesale supplier of fuel to
the Connetic retail fuel site in Armidale.

Competition and Consumer Commission (the ACCC) has considered
the information provided with the notification waiver application and
had regard to the factors in section 51ABV(2)(b) of the Competition

the Acquisition is unlikely to give rise to any material lessening of
competition. In particular:
a. there is no horizontal overlap between Freedom Fuels and
the target in the retail supply of fuel in Armidale or the
surrounding area
b. there are alternative retail suppliers of fuel to customers in
Armidale and the surrounding area
c. there appears to be a low risk of foreclosure or other
concerning vertical effects resulting from exclusionary

Acquisition were put into effect, the notification thresholds

to be notified.

determination_table_content.details:
Ernst & Young (EY Australia) applied for a notification waiver in
respect of its proposed acquisition of 100% of the business and
assets of EY Business Solutions Pty Ltd and EY Identity Pty Ltd
(together, the Australian EY Fusion business), as described in the
documents provided as part of the application (the Acquisition).
The Acquisition will result in the transfer of ownership of the
Australian EY Fusion business from AP Fusion Holdings (Singapore)
Pte Ltd, a wholly owned subsidiary of AP Fusion LP Limited
Partnership which holds such interest on behalf of the Hong Kong,
Korea, Singapore and Malaysia EY member firms (EY selling
member firms).

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission has
determined under section 51ABV(1)(a) of the Competition and
Consumer Act 2010 (Cth) that the Acquisition is not required to be
notified.
3 July 2026

EY Australia (a partnership) forms part of the global EY network. EY
Australia provides professional services including assurance,
consulting, strategy, transactions and tax services in Australia.
The EY Fusion business provides artificial intelligence and data
analytics services, including cybersecurity services, in Australia and
New Zealand. EY Australia provides these services in Australia
through the Australian EY Fusion business.
The EY selling member firms also form part of the global EY network
and provide professional services including assurance, consulting,
strategy, transactions and tax services outside of Australia.

In making this notification waiver determination, the Australian
Competition and Consumer Commission (the ACCC) has considered
the information provided with the notification waiver application and
had regard to the factors in section 51ABV(2)(b) of the Competition
and Consumer Act 2010 (Cth) (the Act).
Based on the information currently before it, the ACCC considers that
the Acquisition is unlikely to give rise to any material lessening of
competition. In particular:
a. the Acquisition effectively represents a reorganisation within
the global EY network and will not involve any change to
market shares or market concentration in Australia
b. there is no competitive overlap between EY Australia and the
Australian EY Fusion business, and the EY selling member
firms, in the supply of artificial intelligence, data analytics
services and cybersecurity services in Australia
c. there are alternative suppliers of artificial intelligence, data
analytics services and cybersecurity services in Australia.
The ACCC has also had regard to the likelihood that, if the
Acquisition were put into effect, the notification thresholds
determined under section 51ABP(1) of the Act would apply.
While the ACCC considers that the notification thresholds are likely
to be met, given that material competition concerns are unlikely to
arise, the ACCC has determined that the Acquisition is not required
to be notified.
The ACCC also considered the potential application of section
51ABD of the Act. However, the applicant submitted that it was not
clear that the Acquisition falls within this provision and having regard
to the particular circumstances, including the consequences of non-
notification in reliance on the exemption if it was found not to apply,
the ACCC considered it appropriate to make a determination on the
basis that the acquisition provisions in the Act apply to the
Acquisition.
The ACCC considers that the determination is consistent with the
object of the Act and the interests of consumers in promoting
competition.
For more information about the ACCC’s approach to considering
notification waiver applications and to assessing competition
effects more generally, see the ACCC’s interim guidance on
notification waivers and merger assessment guidelines.

phase2_notice_matters_to_investigate.heading: Relevant areas of competition
items: The extent to which there are discrete product markets for calibration services within certain testing domains.

The extent to which there are narrower geographic markets within Australia for calibration services in certain testing domains, for example where equipment cannot be transported across significant distances.

Whether certain types of calibration tests need to be performed at a customer’s site, for example because the bulk or sensitivity of the equipment being calibrated means it cannot be transported to the calibration service provider’s laboratory for testing.

items: The extent to which alternative suppliers would meaningfully constrain the merged entity post-Acquisition in the supply of calibration services in certain testing domains, taking into account factors such as their scope of accreditation, breadth of service offering, price and turnaround times, particularly in relation to the following testing domains: electrical, radiofrequency, torque and force.

The extent to which there are specific types of calibration services within relevant testing domains (such as electrical calibration services), in relation to which the Parties may not compete closely and/or there may be effective alternative suppliers.
The likelihood of timely new entry and expansion to constrain the merged entity in the electrical, radiofrequency, torque and force testing domains.

items: The extent to which alternative suppliers would meaningfully constrain the merged entity post-Acquisition in the supply of calibration services across a range of testing domains, taking into account factors such as their scope of accreditation, breadth of service offering, price and turnaround times.

The extent to which customers rely on a calibration service supplier to supply a broad range of calibration services across multiple testing domains, and the extent to which customers can multi-source from various suppliers.

The extent to which multiple suppliers could enter into arrangements that enable a single supplier from the group to offer all of their calibration services, across the range of their testing domains, to customers.
The likelihood of timely new entry and expansion to constrain the merged entity.

phase2_notice_matters_to_investigate.heading: Relevant areas of competition
items: The extent to which there are discrete product markets for calibration services within certain testing domains.

The extent to which there are narrower geographic markets within Australia for calibration services in certain testing domains, for example where equipment cannot be transported across significant distances.

Whether certain types of calibration tests need to be performed at a customer’s site, for example because the bulk or sensitivity of the equipment being calibrated means it cannot be transported to the calibration service provider’s laboratory for testing.

phase2_notice_matters_to_investigate.heading: Competition effects in the supply of calibration services in certain testing domains
items: The extent to which alternative suppliers would meaningfully constrain the merged entity post-Acquisition in the supply of calibration services in certain testing domains, taking into account factors such as their scope of accreditation, breadth of service offering, price and turnaround times, particularly in relation to the following testing domains: electrical, radiofrequency, torque and force.

The extent to which there are specific types of calibration services within relevant testing domains (such as electrical calibration services), in relation to which the Parties may not compete closely and/or there may be effective alternative suppliers.
The likelihood of timely new entry and expansion to constrain the merged entity in the electrical, radiofrequency, torque and force testing domains.

phase2_notice_matters_to_investigate.heading: Competition effects in the supply of calibration services to customers that require multiple calibration services across a range of testing domains
items: The extent to which alternative suppliers would meaningfully constrain the merged entity post-Acquisition in the supply of calibration services across a range of testing domains, taking into account factors such as their scope of accreditation, breadth of service offering, price and turnaround times.

The extent to which customers rely on a calibration service supplier to supply a broad range of calibration services across multiple testing domains, and the extent to which customers can multi-source from various suppliers.

The extent to which multiple suppliers could enter into arrangements that enable a single supplier from the group to offer all of their calibration services, across the range of their testing domains, to customers.
The likelihood of timely new entry and expansion to constrain the merged entity.

phase2_notice_matters_to_investigate.heading: Competitive effects in the supply of calibration services for reference equipment in the electrical testing domain
items: The extent to which alternative suppliers would meaningfully constrain the merged entity post-Acquisition in the supply of calibration services for reference equipment in the electrical testing domain, taking into account factors such as their scope of accreditation, breath of service offering, price and turnaround times.
The likelihood of timely new entry and expansion to constrain the merged entity.

phase2_notice_matters_to_investigate.heading: Relevant areas of competition
items: The appropriate product dimensions of competition in the supply of SURF services to customers in Australia, including the degree to which different pipelay methods are substitutable.

phase2_notice_matters_to_investigate.heading: Competition effects in the supply of SURF services
items: The geographic and technical conditions relevant to Australian SURF projects and how these affect the selection of pipelaying vessels and SURF service providers.
The likely effect of the removal of a key provider on competition in the supply of SURF services in Australia.

The likely extent to which remaining SURF service suppliers would meaningfully constrain the merged entity in relation to tenders in Australia, taking into account their current and prospective capability and geographic areas of operation.

The extent to which operators of Australian offshore projects could credibly threaten to bypass the merged firm, either by self-supplying some or all SURF services and/or sponsoring new entry or expansion.
The likelihood of timely and sufficient new entry, and consequent participation in Australian SURF project tenders, if the Acquisition proceeds.
